title: What to watch, read and wear as technology melts down | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

With modern systems seeminglyon the verge of collapse, an apocalypse story can be weirdly comforting, or even romantic. Just listen to “As The World Falls Down,” David Bowie’s sparkling ballad inflected with longing from the delightful 1986 film “Labyrinth”:

Every thrill is gone

Wasn’t too much fun at all,

But I’ll be there for you

As the world falls down.

I wish we could have the late singer here for us right now. In the past few weeks, it’s felt a little bit like the world really is falling down.

First there was a Microsoft outage, then a nationwide ground stop, only the second since 9/11. Then, digital systems seemed to fall like dominos, with outages at United Airlines, a variety of banks, another at Microsoft, and even at the NSA. As my colleague David Goldmanwrote, “The internet is held together with shoestring and bubblegum.” The weird sequence of failures have emphasized just how fragile our digital world is — and sent some people pondering whether this is the end of the world as we know it.

So what can we do with all this angst and anxiety besides buy extra batteries and horde cash in our mattresses? Why not enjoy it a little? We’ve compiled a mixtape of sorts to get you through our era of precarity: books, movies, even some travel and snack recommendations as we brace for the potential collapse of our fragile digital ecosystem.

We’ve been drawn to tales of doom for centuries, ranging from stories of torrential, civilization-ending floods that pop up in many religious traditions to apocalyptic survival films like “Independence Day” and “Terminator 2: Judgment Day.” It’s both frightening and reassuring to remember that everything can change and be remade anew.

In the world of classics, the original“Planet of the Apes”is a true apocalypse film, taking place in a far-off future after human society has collapsed, creating the perfect vacuum for simian takeover. There’s“The War of the Worlds,”H.G. Wells’ serialized turn-of-the-century novel about an alien invasion. The novel is so realistic — and so frightening — that when it was broadcast on the radio by legendary actor and director Orson Welles, it induced genuine panic from some people who thought the aliens were really invading.

Cormac McCarthy’s“The Road”is a 2006 post-apocalyptic novel that won the Pulitzer for fiction for its gritty portrayal of a father and son surviving after an extinction-level event, and it was adapted into a 2009 film starring Viggo Mortensen and Charlize Theron. The science fiction writer Octavia Butler also visualized a post-apocalyptic United States in“The Parable of the Sower,”a 1993 novel set in – gasp! – 2024 that explores climate change and social inequality.

Master postmodernist Don DeLillo seemed to foreshadow the current moment with“The Silence,”his 2020 novel about what would happen if the world’s electronic systems all failed. (Other quasi-apocalyptic disasters explored in past DeLillo works include industrial accidents in “White Noise” and nuclear proliferation in “Underworld.”)

Another frighteningly prescient vision of possible apocalypse emerged in Ling Ma’s novel“Severance,”in which a mysterious airborne disease causes modern society to collapse. The novel was published just two years before the Covid-19 pandemic would trigger a very real global shutdown.

In other iterations of possible apocalypse that feel disturbingly real, artists have envisioned the disasters that could be wrought by the climate crisis.

The Korean filmmaker Bong Joon Ho placed the survivors of the apocalypse — including Chris Evans — inside a claustrophobic never-ending train ride for“Snowpiercer,”his 2013 English-language debut about the social inequalities exacerbated by climate collapse. This year’s criminally underrated“Digger,”too, represents a modern version of earthly destruction triggered by greedy capitalists and climate disaster. Latvia’s Oscar-winning“Flow,”an animated film with no dialogue, presents a sweeter, cuter but no less riveting post-apocalyptic vision (I promise!).

There is only one apocalypse TV series to rule them all:“The Leftovers,”which premiered in 2014 and ran for three glorious seasons, starring Carrie Coon and Justin Theroux. Based on Tom Perotta’s 2011 novel of the same name, the series suggests how a tiny change can dramatically unravel the world. What would happen, it asks, if 2% of the world’s population vanished? “The Leftovers” doesn’t present a blood-and-doom apocalypse, but it’s still a radically altered version of the world, one where new religions and traditions have sprouted to account for the mysterious absence of parents, friends, lovers. (Other notably beloved apocalypse series include“Station 11”and“The Last of Us.”) (These three TV shows are streamable on HBO Max, which is owned by CNN’s parent company.)

On the unscripted side, there’s National Geographic’s“Doomsday Preppers,”a reality series that ran from 2012 to 2014 and profiles survivalists planning for disaster. You can take some notes before the electricity goes out and the banks shut down.

What to listen to as the world falls down? David Bowie, obviously. And a shoutout here belongs to the gritty,nostalgic soundtrack to “Yellowjackets,”which features ‘90s classics like Mazzy Star’s “Fade Into You” and Elliott Smith’s “Pitseleh.” The series itself is a “Lord of the Flies”-esque apocalyptic vision of a plane crash that deposits a high school girls’ soccer team in the remote wilderness.

Other obvious apocalypse tracks are Weyes Blood’s“And in the Darkness, Hearts Aglow” and R.E.M’s“It’s the End of the World as We Know It (And I Feel Fine).”

These songs all have a nostalgic feel. But I also think the end of the world might sound like… hyperpop? The distorted music of artists likeGrimes,SophieandSlayyytersound like the future to me – maybe the future even after everything we know collapses.

But what will we eat when the world around us falls to pieces? In “Snowpiercer,” the apocalypse’s survivors subsist on unappetizing rectangular bars of protein amalgamated from cockroaches. In real life, we haveTwinkies, which are tastier than cockroach bars andjust as indestructible.

The very trendy“David” protein barsalso seem like they might sustain you through societal collapse.

And although I haven’t seen cockroach products marketed yet, ithasbeen predicted thatinsect protein– like grasshopper flour – will become increasingly popular in the coming decades.

In 2010, the legendary British fashion designer Alexander McQueen released a collection he said was inspired by his vision of the end of the world — and a return to the sea.

“Humankind is made up of creatures that evolved from the sea, and we may be heading back to an underwater future as the ice cap dissolves,” the designer said ina press releaseat the time.

The collection featured reptilian patterns onmicro dresses and fabrics mimicking the skin of aquatic mammals. It’s a somewhat optimistic, if wet, vision of the post-apocalyptic future.

In more recent trends, the explosion ofRealTree camopatterns this year feels like an omen of apocalyptic anxiety. What better than camo to hide from zombies or aliens in?

Where to go when the world ends? Maybe we should look to the billionaires, who have shelled out for extraordinarily luxe apocalypse bunkers in remote locations. Mark Zuckerberg’s is, allegedly, underneath his ranch on the Hawaiian islandKauai; Peter Thiel tried but failed to build one in New Zealand.

I also keep thinking aboutEaster Island— also known asRapa Nui— the extremely remote Chilean territory that serves as the setting for Martin McDonagh’s newest film, “Wild Horse Nine.” The movie isn’t an apocalypse story by any means (though it does involve beginnings and endings). But it depicts the unique pleasures and struggles of being very, very far away from the rest of the world.

Experts have offered reassurance that despite appearances, our current cascade of tech breakdowns are just symptoms of old, failing systems, not of a coordinated breakdown. At least when the grid fails us, we’ll have some good content about it to turn to.
